gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured brightness for any screen it recommended. Two named reviewers did measure two of them. ITPro measured the Dell Pro 14 Plus (P1425) at 486.75 cd/m² peak and 96.4% sRGB coverage. Parkablogs measured the original Mobile Pixels Duex Plus at 152 nits and 68% sRGB, about half the 300-nit rating Mobile Pixels gives the Duex Plus line.
standout_why: I compared against three cited rivals. itechguides' '15 Best Laptop Screen Extenders for 2026' (opened 2026-11-21) gives only maker or Amazon-seller figures, such as Mobile Pixels' 300-nit spec for the Duex Max DS and its '300-nit, 60 Hz class' for the Duex Plus DS. The page itself says no figure was measured by a named tester. Macworld's 'Best Portable Monitors for Mac 2026' (Simon Jary, updated 2026-10-16) lists 'Up to' brightness and sRGB specs without saying how any were measured, and it does not cover the Duex Plus DS, UPERFECT or Dell P1425. TechRepublic's page (cited) returned HTTP 403 in English and Spanish, so I could not check it. A search snippet suggests it quotes a Tom's Hardware figure of 409 nits for an unnamed business monitor, which may be the Dell P1425. This is unverified, so the standout score assumes TechRepublic may carry part of the Dell figure. PCWorld's guide (Matthew S. Smith, updated 2026-06-26) has measured figures, but none for the Duex, UPERFECT, Dell P1425 or FOPO. I could not open RTINGS (its body did not load), Wired (fetch refused) or 3DTested (HTTP 525).
decides: This confirms ChatGPT's 'standalone 14-inch' advice and weakens its 'Duex Plus DS for everyday campus use' pick. Students work under library and classroom lighting. The one named measurement of a Duex Plus is 152 nits, while the Dell 14-inch standalone measured 486.75 cd/m², about 3.2 times as bright. The Duex figure is from 2022 on the original Duex Plus, not the DS, so the page should present it as that model's figure and not as the DS's. For the screens we link (Duex Max DS, FOPO S1/S7), I found no named measurement, so their rows should carry the maker's brightness claim marked as a claim. Compatibility (native USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode versus a driver, and the base-MacBook one-display limit) still decides most picks. Measured brightness is the second figure the ranking can use.

findings.label: Peak brightness, measured by ITPro (Bobby Hellard)
findings.source_title: Dell Pro 14 Plus monitor review: A little efficient monitor for the roaming worker (ITPro)
findings.note: Quote: 'we recorded its peak brightness at 486.75 cd/m2'. The page says 'last updated 2 June 2025' and gives no original publication date. Dell's own rating, from retailer spec listings, is 400 nits, so ITPro measured above the rating.

findings.label: Colour gamut, measured by ITPro (colorimeter + DisplayCAL)
findings.source_title: Dell Pro 14 Plus monitor review: A little efficient monitor for the roaming worker (ITPro)
findings.note: Quote: 'with our colorimeter and DisplayCal is showcased 96.4% for gamut color coverage (98% for volume)'. ITPro also reports a macOS problem: on a MacBook Pro, the extra display in portrait mode appeared only as a small window. Both USB-C ports carry DisplayPort and up to 65 W power delivery, and there is no HDMI. Weight in ITPro's spec table is 0.56 kg; this is a spec, not a measurement.

findings.product: Mobile Pixels Duex Plus (original, not the DS revision)
findings.label: Max brightness and sRGB coverage, measured by Parkablogs (Teoh Yi Chie)
findings.source_title: Review: Duex Plus portable display attachment for laptops (Parkablogs)
findings.note: Quote: 'With a colour calibrator, I measured colour support for just 68% sRGB and a maximum brightness of 152 nits.' The calibrator model is not named. The review was published 2022-07-12 and covers the original Duex Plus. The Duex Plus DS that ChatGPT showed is a later revision, and I found no measurement of it. Comparison: 486.75 ÷ 152 ≈ 3.2 times the Dell's measured peak.

findings.note: Quote: 'The weight is 1.3lbs (589g).' The review does not say whether the unit was weighed or the figure taken from the spec sheet. It is close to ChatGPT's 'approximately 1.3 lb' for the DS.

unsourced: Measured brightness or gamut for the Mobile Pixels Duex Max DS. Amateur Photographer's Duex Max review reportedly measured 64% sRGB with a Datacolor Spyder X2, according to a search snippet, but both of its URLs returned HTTP 403. Root Nation's Duex Max DS review also returned 403. I found no RTINGS, Notebookcheck, Tom's Hardware or PCWorld measurement of the Duex Max.

RTINGS' Duex Plus measurements: a search snippet gives 166 cd/m² and 64.4% sRGB, but the review body did not load through fetch on rtings.com/monitor/reviews/mobile-pixels/duex-plus or on the compare page. GadgetReview's Duex Plus page lists 178 nits, 1,157:1 and 60% sRGB without saying who measured them. Its own sections disagree (185 nits, 979:1, 64.4% sRGB), and its text appears to summarise other reviewers, so I left it out.
Measured figures for the UPERFECT 14-inch 2K swivel extender. A search found only retailer listings, which disagree with each other: 300 vs 400 nits, and 2240×1400 vs 2160×1440.
Measured figures for the FOPO S1 and S7. No named-reviewer measurement appeared in the searches I ran, and I did not run a FOPO-specific search within the call budget.

3DTested/Tom's Hardware's Dell P1425 review (409 nits, per a snippet) returned HTTP 525. The TechRepublic cited page returned 403 in English and Spanish. RTINGS' Dell P1425 figures did not load. Wired's guide could not be fetched.
Measured figures for the Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro. Macworld lists only specs: 300 nits, 100% sRGB and 4.13 lb, with no measurement method stated.
